{{Short description|Field of radiation}}
[[File:Airy.gif|thumb|Evolution of an Airy beam.]]
An '''Airy beam''' is a propagation invariant wave whose main intensity lobe propagates along a curved parabolic trajectory while being resilient to perturbations (self-healing).

==Physical description==
A cross section of an ideal Airy beam would reveal an area of principal intensity, with a series of adjacent, less luminous areas trailing off to infinity. In reality, the beam is truncated so as to have a finite composition.

As the beam propagates, it does not diffract, i.e., does not spread out. The Airy beam also has the characteristic of freely accelerating. As it propagates, it bends so as to form a parabolic arc.

==History==
The term "Airy beam" derives from the Airy integral, developed in the 1830s by [[Sir George Biddell Airy]] to explain [[optical caustics]] such as those appearing in a [[rainbow]].<ref name="physorg.com">[http://www.physorg.com/news115556629.html "Scientists make first observation of Airy optical beams"]</ref>

The Airy waveform was first theorized in 1979 by [[M. V. Berry]] and [[Nandor Balazs|Nándor L. Balázs]]. They demonstrated a nonspreading Airy [[wave packet]] solution to the time--dependent [[Schrödinger equation]] for the wavefunction <math>\psi(x,t)</math> of a [[free particle]] moving in one spatial dimension, <math>x</math> in time, <math>t</math>.<ref name="B&B">{{cite journal |last1=Berry |first1=M. V. |last2=Balázs |first2=Nándor L. |year=1979 |title=Nonspreading wave packets |doi=10.1119/1.11855 |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=47 |issue=3 |pages=264–267 |bibcode=1979AmJPh..47..264B}}</ref>  The probability density, <math>|\psi(x,t)|^2</math>, that is associated with this solution exhibits uniform acceleration in <math>x</math> with time <math>t</math>.   
 
In 2007 researchers from the [[University of Central Florida]] ([[United States]]) were able to create and observe an Airy beam for the first time in both one- and two-dimensional configurations. The members of the team were Georgios Siviloglou, John Broky, Aristide Dogariu, and [[Demetrios N. Christodoulides|Demetrios Christodoulides]].<ref name=siviloglou07a>{{cite journal | last1 = Siviloglou | first1 = G. A. | last2 = Broky | first2 = J. | last3 = Dogariu | first3 = A. | last4 = Christodoulides | first4 = D. N. | year = 2007 | title = Observation of Accelerating Airy Beams | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.213901 | pmid = 18233219 | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 99 | issue = 21| article-number = 213901 | bibcode=2007PhRvL..99u3901S}}</ref>

In one-dimension, the Airy beam is the only exactly shape-preserving accelerating solution to the free-particle Schrödinger equation (or 2D paraxial wave equation). However, in two dimensions (or 3D paraxial systems), two separable solutions are possible: two-dimensional Airy beams and accelerating parabolic beams.<ref name="ApA">{{cite journal | last1 = Bandres | first1 = M.A. | year = 2008 | title = Accelerating parabolic beams | url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/11573/1/BANol08b.pdf| journal = Opt. Lett. | volume = 33 | issue = 15| pages = 1678–1680 | doi = 10.1364/OL.33.001678 | pmid = 18670501 |bibcode = 2008OptL...33.1678B}}</ref> Furthermore, it has been shown<ref name="AcB">{{cite journal | last1 = Bandres | first1 = M. A. | year = 2009 | title = Accelerating beams | journal = Opt. Lett. | volume = 34 | issue = 24| pages = 3791–3793 | doi = 10.1364/OL.34.003791 | pmid = 20016615 |bibcode = 2009OptL...34.3791B| url = https://authors.library.caltech.edu/17176/ }}</ref> that any function on the real line can be mapped to an accelerating beam with a different transverse shape.

In 2018, scientists determined the cubic phase of Airy beams in a system analogous to [[surface gravity]] water-waves. Using an external hydrodynamic linear potential, they were also able to decelerate the Airy beam analog and halt the self-accelerating front of the Airy beam.
<ref name=Rozenman2019>{{cite journal |last=G. G. Rozenman |first=A. Arie |author2=W. P. Schleich, L. Shemer, M. Zimmerman, M. A. ==Mathematical description==

Using the notation of the original treatment of,<ref name="B&B" /> we consider solutions <math>\psi(x,t)</math> of the [[Schrödinger equation]] 
for a particle of mass <math>m</math> evolving freely in time, <math>t</math>, along a one-dimensional spatial coordinate, <math>x</math>:


<math>i \hbar\frac{\partial \psi(x,t)}{\partial t} =  -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2 \psi(x,t)}{\partial x^2} </math>,

where <math>\hbar = h/(2 \pi)</math> is the reduced [[Planck constant]] and <math>i</math> is the [[imaginary unit]].


As shown in,<ref name="B&B" /> a solution to that equation is


<math>\psi(x,t) = \mathrm{Ai} \left[ \frac{B}{\hbar^{2/3}} \left( x - \frac{B^3 t^2}{4 m^2}\right) \right] e^{\left( i \frac{B^3 t}{2 m \hbar} \right) [x - ( \frac{B^3 t^2}{6 m^2} )]}</math>,

where <math>\mathrm{Ai}</math> is the [[Airy function]] and <math>B</math> is chosen so as to fit initial conditions at <math>t = 0</math>. It is evident from this expression that the profile <math>|\psi(x,t)|^2</math> undergoes uniform acceleration at a rate of <math>a = B^3/(2m^2)</math>.

In actual experimental practice, Airy beams of light, electrons and neutrons have been approximated by programming wavefunctions with spatial light modulation or diffractive elements.

==Experimental observation==

Georgios Sivilioglou, et al. successfully fabricated an Airy beam in 2007. A beam with a [[Gaussian distribution]] was modulated by a [[spatial light modulator]] to have an Airy distribution. The result was recorded by a [[CCD camera]].<ref name="physorg.com" /><ref name="siviloglou07a" /> 

Airy beams of electrons were demonstrated in 2013 by Voloch-Bloch, et al., using diffraction of electrons by a nanoscale hologram.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Voloch-Bloch|first1=Noa|last2=Lereah|first2=Yossi|last3=Lilach|first3=Yigal|last4=Gover|first4=Avraham|last5=Arie|first5=Ady|date=2013|title=Generation of electron Airy beams|journal=Nature|volume=494|page=331|doi=10.1038/nature11840|arxiv=1205.2112}}</ref> 

In 2024, Airy beams of neutrons with de Broglie wavelength 1.2 nm were demonstrated at the GPSANS [[small-angle neutron scattering]] beamline at the [[High Flux Isotope Reactor]] of [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite journal
|last1=Sarenac|first1=Dusan
|last2=Lailey|first2=Owen
|last3=Henderson|first3=Melissa E.
|last4=Ekinci|first4=Huseyin
|last5=Clark|first5=Charles W.
|last6=Cory|first6=David G.  
|last7=DeBeer-Schmitt|first7=Lisa
|last8=Huber|first8=Michael G.
|last9=White|first9=Jonathan S. 
|last10=Zhernenkov|first10=Kirill
|last11=Pushin|first11=Dmitry A.
|date=2025
|title=Generation of Neutron Airy Beams
|journal=Physical Review Letters
|volume=134
|article-number=153401
|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.153401|arxiv=2407.19384}}
</ref>
The neutron beam was diffracted by
an array of 6,250,000 individual 1{{mu}}m &times; 1{{mu}}m phase gratings
fabricated on a 0.25 cm<sup>2</sup> silicon chip; Airy beam profiles were observed after flight paths between 10 and 20 m.
In this experiment, Airy diffraction is mediated by the [[strong interaction]] between a low-energy neutron and the silicon nuclei,
vs. the electromagnetic interaction that governs optical and [[electron diffraction]].



  

== Modified Airy beams ==

=== Attenuation-compensation ===
Beams may encounter losses as they travel through materials which will cause attenuation of the beam intensity. A property common to non-diffracting (or propagation-invariant) beams, such as the Airy beam and [[Bessel beam]], is the ability to control the longitudinal intensity envelope of the beam without significantly altering the other characteristics of the beam. This can be used to create Airy beams which grow in intensity at they travel and can be used to counteract losses, therefore maintaining a beam of constant intensity as it propagates.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schley|first1=Ran|last2=Kaminer|first2=Ido|last3=Greenfield|first3=Elad|last4=Bekenstein|first4=Rivka|last5=Lumer|first5=Yaakov|last6=Segev|first6=Mordechai|date=2014|title=Loss-proof self-accelerating beams and their use in non-paraxial manipulation of particles' trajectories|journal=Nature Communications|volume=5|page=5189|doi=10.1038/ncomms6189|pmid=25355605|bibcode=2014NatCo...5.5189S|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Preciado|first1=Miguel A.|last2=Dholakia|first2=Kishan|last3=Mazilu|first3=Michael|date=2014-08-15|title=Generation of attenuation-compensating Airy beams|journal=Optics Letters|language=EN|volume=39|issue=16|pages=4950–4953|doi=10.1364/ol.39.004950|pmid=25121916|bibcode=2014OptL...39.4950P|hdl=10023/7244|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://gist.github.com/mpreciado/115637b0d557a4eb8b7a1a0723308119 |title=GitHub Matlab/Octave code: Compensating Airy beam for diffractive light delivery control}}</ref> In temporal domain, an analogous modified dispersion-free attenuation-compensating Airy-based ("rocket") pulse was previously proposed and demonstrated in,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Preciado|first1=Miguel A.|last2=Sugden|first2=Miguel|date=2012-12-01|title=Proposal and design of Airy-based rocket pulses for invariant propagation in lossy dispersive media|journal=Optics Letters|language=EN|volume=37|issue=23|pages=4970–4972|doi=10.1364/OL.37.004970|pmid=23202107|bibcode=2012OptL...37.4970P|url=https://publications.aston.ac.uk/id/eprint/25878/1/airy.pdf}}</ref> designed to compensate media losses as it propagates through dispersive media.

==Applications==

=== Optical trapping and manipulation ===
Researchers at the [[University of St. Andrews]] have used Airy beams to manipulate small particles, moving them along curves and around corners. This may find use in fields such as microfluidic engineering and cell biology.<ref>[http://www.physorg.com/news141924149.html "Light throws a curve ball"]</ref> 
Significant theoretical works have been also undertaken by F.G. Mitri and his collaborators both in optics and acoustics, and related works can be found in these references: [https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4962397 Airy acoustical–sheet spinner tweezers]; [https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5005088 Acoustics of finite asymmetric exotic beams: Examples of Airy and fractional Bessel beams]; [https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4982784 Pulling and spinning reversal of a sub-wavelength absorptive sphere in adjustable vector Airy light-sheets]; [https://doi.org/10.1140/epjd/e2017-80632-5 Adjustable vector Airy light-sheet single optical tweezers: negative radiation forces on a subwavelength spheroid and spin torque reversal]; [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jqsrt.2020.106853 Optical radiation force on a dielectric sphere of arbitrary size illuminated by a linearly polarized Airy light-sheet]; [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jqsrt.2020.107327 Optical torque on an absorptive dielectric sphere of arbitrary size illuminated by a linearly-polarized Airy light-sheet]; [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jqsrt.2020.107466 Circularly-polarized Airy light-sheet spinner tweezers and particle transport]

(see also: [[Optical tweezers]])

=== Imaging and microscopy ===
Researchers at the [[University of St. Andrews]] have further utilised Airy beams to make a large field of view (FOV) while maintaining high axial contrast in a [[Light sheet fluorescence microscopy|light-sheet microscope]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Vettenburg|first1=Tom|last2=Dalgarno|first2=Heather I C|last3=Nylk|first3=Jonathan|last4=Coll-Lladó|first4=Clara|last5=Ferrier|first5=David E K|last6=Čižmár|first6=Tomáš|last7=Gunn-Moore|first7=Frank J|last8=Dholakia|first8=Kishan|title=Light-sheet microscopy using an Airy beam|journal=Nature Methods|volume=11|issue=5|pages=541–544|doi=10.1038/nmeth.2922|pmid=24705473|year=2014|hdl=10023/5521|s2cid=205422713 |url=https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/10023/5521/1/airsheet_preproof.pdf|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2014/title,241160,en.php |title=Imaging turns a corner |access-date=2014-04-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140426235410/http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2014/title,241160,en.php |archive-date=2014-04-26 }}</ref> This technique has been adapted to use [[Multiphoton excitation microscopy|multi-photon excitation]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Piksarv|first1=Peeter|last2=Marti|first2=Dominik|last3=Le|first3=Tuan|last4=Unterhuber|first4=Angelika|last5=Forbes|first5=Lindsay H.|last6=Andrews|first6=Melissa R. Andrews|last7=Stingl|first7=Andreas|last8=Drexler|first8=Wolfgang|last9=Andersen|first9=Peter E.|date=2017|title=Integrated single- and two-photon light sheet microscopy using accelerating beams|journal=Scientific Reports|volume=7|issue=1|page=1435|doi=10.1038/s41598-017-01543-4|doi-access=free|pmid=28469191|pmc=5431168|bibcode=2017NatSR...7.1435P}}</ref> and attenuation-compensated Airy beams<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nylk|first1=Jonathan|last2=McCluskey|first2=Kaley|last3=Preciado|first3=Miguel A.|last4=Mazilu|first4=Michael|last5=Yang|first5=Zhengyi|last6=Gunn-Moore|first6=Frank J.|last7=Aggarwal|first7=Sanya|last8=Tello|first8=Javier A.|last9=Ferrier|first9=David E. K.|date=2018-04-01|title=Light-sheet microscopy with attenuation-compensated propagation-invariant beams|journal=Science Advances|language=en|volume=4|issue=4|article-number=eaar4817|doi=10.1126/sciadv.aar4817|pmid=29740614|pmc=5938225|arxiv=1708.02612|bibcode= 2018SciA....4.4817N}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Veettikazhy|first1=Madhu|last2=Nylk|first2=Jonathan|last3=Gasparoli|first3=Federico|last4=Escobet-Montalbán|first4=Adrià|last5=Hansen|first5=Anders Kragh|last6=Marti|first6=Dominik|last7=Andersen|first7=Peter Eskil|last8=Dholakia|first8=Kishan|date=2020-05-15|title=Multi-photon attenuation-compensated light-sheet fluorescence microscopy|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=10|issue=1|page=8090 |doi=10.1038/s41598-020-64891-8|pmid=32415135 |pmc=7229186 |bibcode=2020NatSR..10.8090V |issn=2045-2322|doi-access=free}}</ref> to achieve imaging at greater depths within biological specimens.

=== Micro-machining ===
The accelerating and diffraction-free features of the Airy wavepacket have also been utilized by researchers at the [[University of Crete]] to produce two-dimensional, circular-Airy waves, termed abruptly-autofocusing beams.<ref name="Efremidis2010AAF">{{cite journal|last=Efremidis|first=Nikolaos|author2=Christodoulides, Demetrios|title=Abruptly autofocusing waves|journal=Optics Letters|year=2010|volume=35|issue=23|pages=4045–7|doi=10.1364/OL.35.004045|pmid=21124607|bibcode = 2010OptL...35.4045E|s2cid=300877 |url=http://preprints.acmac.uoc.gr/33/1/acmac-0033.pdf}}</ref> These beams tend to focus in an abrupt fashion shortly before a target while maintaining a constant and low intensity profile along the propagated path and can be useful in laser [[microfabrication]]<ref name="Papazoglou2011">{{cite journal|last=Papazoglou|first=Dimitrios|author2=Efremidis, Nikolaos|author3= Christodoulides, Demetrios|author4= Tzortzakis, Stelios|s2cid=9384164|title=Observation of abruptly autofocusing waves|journal=Optics Letters|year=2011|volume=36|issue=10|pages=1842–4|doi=10.1364/OL.36.001842 |pmid=21593909 |bibcode=2011OptL...36.1842P}}</ref> or medical laser treatments.
